findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=1.00): predict_timeline_edit
findings.detail: The description of 'premiere-pro-mcp.predict_timeline_edit' scores 1.00 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: encoded_blob. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: encoded_blob, imperative_density, entropy.

evidence.description: Predict exact affected clips for a conservative supported insert/overwrite/trim/split/move/remove/ripple/enable subset using complete canonical state. Refuses unknown locks, links, source handles and retiming. Local prediction does not execute Premiere or promise native edit semantics.

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'premiere-pro-mcp': executes commands + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 12 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and can reach the network, which is remote code execution with a delivery channel rather than a hint of one. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'premiere-pro-mcp': executes commands + writes or deletes files
findings.detail: 312 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another writes or deletes files. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and writes files, so the agent can persist a payload for a later session to pick up. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'agentistics__mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends email or messages
findings.detail: 9 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends email or messages. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send mail. This is the postmark-mcp shape: the mail tool was legitimate, the credentials were reachable, and the combination was the incident. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'cyanheads__git-mcp-server': executes commands + writes or deletes files
findings.detail: 2 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another writes or deletes files. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and writes files, so the agent can persist a payload for a later session to pick up. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and writes files, so the agent can persist a payload for a later session to pick up. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.

findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: @haven_ai/mcp
findings.detail: 'haven_ai__mcp' launches @haven_ai/mcp through npx without a version. The client resolves the version at start time, so any future publish to that package name runs with your credentials. This is how postmark-mcp (Sept 2025) reached roughly 300 organisations.
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version and an integrity hash: "args": ["@haven_ai/mcp@<version>"] and drop the -y flag. Re-pin deliberately, after reviewing the diff.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'doitintl__doit-mcp-server': executes commands + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 718 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and can reach the network, which is remote code execution with a delivery channel rather than a hint of one. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

evidence.description: Sales and Trends 리포트 = **실매출의 기준선** — GET /v1/salesReports (gzip TSV 를 파싱해 돌려준다). 분석 이벤트(GA4 in_app_purchase 등)로 매출을 세면 안 되는 이유가 여기 있다: TestFlight·Xcode 설치의 결제는 **sandbox 라 청구가 0원인데도** 클라이언트에는 성공한 결제로 보여 이벤트가 그대로 나간다. 이 리포트에는 sandbox 가 애초에 들어오지 않으므로, 둘을 비교하면 "진짜 돈이 들어온 건수"가 곧바로 갈린다. ⚠️ **Developer Proceeds 는 1개당 금액이다** — 총액은 units 를 곱해야 한다(이 도구는 곱해서 준다). ⚠️ 환불은 units 가 **음수**로 들어와 합계에서 상쇄된다. 즉 합계는 순매출이다. ⚠️ 데이터가 없는 날짜는 Apple 이 404 를 주므로 datesWithoutData 로 따로 돌려준다 — "매출 0" 과 "리포트 미생성/설정 오류"를 섞지 말

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'yoonion__mimi-seed-mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends email or messages
findings.detail: 14 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends email or messages. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send mail. This is the postmark-mcp shape: the mail tool was legitimate, the credentials were reachable, and the combination was the incident. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=1.00): create_webhook
findings.detail: The description of 'cito-mcp.create_webhook' scores 1.00 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: credentials+fs_targets. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: cross_tool, fs_targets, entropy, log_len.

evidence.description: Create a webhook on this account: Cito starts POSTing the chosen events to the URL. Needs Pro or Scale; a plan error includes the upgrade link to relay. The URL must be public. The account owner is emailed. webhook.secret comes back ONCE: have the user store it in an environment variable such as CITO_WEBHOOK_SECRET, and do not repeat it in chat. Then call test_webhook. API calls: 1.

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'limostudio-mcp': executes commands + writes or deletes files
findings.detail: 8 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another writes or deletes files. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and writes files, so the agent can persist a payload for a later session to pick up. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'specguard-mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 42 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send data to an address it controls. A single prompt is enough to turn 'summarise this config' into a credential leak. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

evidence.description: An HTTP request as a sequence step: node sends it from the server process (no browser, cookies or CORS); browser runs fetch() inside a connected tab (its cookies, session and origin).

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'devharness': executes commands + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 2 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and can reach the network, which is remote code execution with a delivery channel rather than a hint of one. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'ferrlabs__mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends email or messages
findings.detail: 7 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends email or messages. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send mail. This is the postmark-mcp shape: the mail tool was legitimate, the credentials were reachable, and the combination was the incident. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=0.99): place_image
findings.detail: The description of 'layoutbridge-spm.place_image' scores 0.99 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: hidden_recipient. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: hidden_recipient, entropy, log_len.

evidence.description: Place an image or PDF file (real path on the InDesign machine) into a graphic frame, replacing whatever it held (crop and scale are reset – to merely swap the file use relink_links). fit: fill_proportionally, fit_proportionally, fit_content_to_frame or center_content; without it the frame fitting options of the frame apply. pdf_crop chooses the PDF page box: media (InDesign default – the whole sheet including printer marks, the usual reason for misplaced ads), crop, trim, bleed (for bleed ads),

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'gemmein__mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 1 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send data to an address it controls. A single prompt is enough to turn 'summarise this config' into a credential leak. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'crawlora-mcp': executes commands + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 588 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and can reach the network, which is remote code execution with a delivery channel rather than a hint of one. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.

findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: @us-all/datadog-mcp
